The steep front-to-back (z) direction is heavily foreshortened, so the start sits on a compressed near edge, and the zigzag across the narrow side of the bowl (the main thing to see) is squashed flat. The bowl also fills only about 45% of the frame, with a lot of empty white space. Move the camera higher and more overhead, and closer, so the z direction reads clearly and the bowl fills the view.

plan.title: Stochastic gradient descent on a noisy loss surface
plan.description: A ball sits on a stretched bowl-shaped loss surface (a loss surface shows the error for every pair of two model settings) with a marked minimum at the bottom. Each step, the ball moves against a noisy estimate of the slope and leaves a trail. Two arrows on the ball show the true downhill direction and the noisy step direction, so you can see the ball zigzag toward the bottom and then jitter around it. Change the learning rate and the mini-batch size to see when the path is smooth, noisy, slow or unstable.
plan.reason: The main idea of stochastic gradient descent is how step size and noise shape the path. Changing them yourself and comparing trails on the same surface shows this better than watching one fixed run.
interactions: Play, pause or step the descent one update at a time; a run stops after 200 steps
Drag the ball to a new starting point on the surface before a run
Raise the learning rate: steps get longer and zigzag across the narrow side of the bowl; above 0.5 each swing grows until the ball hits the edge and stops with a 'diverged' readout
Raise the mini-batch size: the noisy arrow stays closer to the true downhill arrow, so the trail gets smoother and settles closer to the bottom
Turn on the full-batch path to see a noise-free gradient descent trail from the same start
Clear trails: removes the drawn paths and sends the ball back to its start point, keeping your current settings
assumptions: Illustration: the loss surface is a made-up formula and the noise is simulated, not from real training data.
The loss is the bowl 0.5·(x² + 4y²), which is steeper in one direction than the other, with its minimum at the centre.
Each noisy gradient is the true slope plus random noise whose size shrinks with one over the square root of the mini-batch size, which copies how averaging more samples reduces noise.
The noise comes from a fixed seed, so pressing Reset replays the same sequence of noisy steps.
The update is plain stochastic gradient descent: new position = old position − learning rate × noisy gradient, with no momentum and no learning-rate decay.
Readouts show the step number, the loss at the ball's current position, and the size of the noise in the current step.
The trail draws one marker every 2 steps, at most 100 markers; every step still runs.
limitations: Changed: the trail draws 100 markers, one every 2 steps, instead of 200; every step still runs.
A single step can raise the loss. The loss only goes down on average, so the loss readout will sometimes go up.
With a fixed learning rate the ball keeps jittering near the minimum and never settles exactly on it. Even at a mini-batch size of 64, a small amount of noise remains.
Real loss surfaces have millions of dimensions and are not simple bowls. This surface has no local minima or saddle points.
On this bowl, the 0.5 threshold for divergence is exact for the noise-free update. Real models have no single threshold you can read off this easily.
plan.learningGoal: Stochastic gradient descent uses a noisy slope estimate from a mini-batch: the learning rate sets how far each step goes and how stable the path is, and the batch size sets how noisy it is.

draft.title: Stochastic gradient descent on a stretched loss bowl
draft.description: A blue bowl-shaped loss surface, steeper front-to-back than side-to-side, has a dark dot at its lowest point. A red ball is the current guess. On each step it moves by the learning rate times a noisy slope estimate, leaving an orange trail. A grey arrow shows the step the true slope would give. An orange arrow shows the actual noisy step. You can also show a dark noise-free path from the same start. Readouts show the loss, the status, the step count and the noise size.
assumptions: Illustration: the loss surface is a made-up formula and the noise is simulated, not from real training data.

Loss = 0.5·(x² + 4y²), drawn at 0.15 × loss over a 5 × 5 square (y runs front to back). It is steeper front to back. The minimum is at the centre. Noise-free steps diverge exactly when the learning rate is above 0.5.
Noisy gradient = true slope + Gaussian noise with spread 2/√(batch size) in each direction. The noise is fixed by the step number, so Reset and Clear trails replay the same noise.

Update: new position = old − learning rate × noisy gradient, with no momentum and no decay. Both arrows show learning rate × gradient (true or noisy), drawn 2× scale. Noise in next step is the noise of the step the orange arrow shows.

A run stops after 200 steps: converged if the loss is below 0.5, otherwise stopped. Diverged means the ball left the drawn surface; the ball and trail are then drawn at the surface edge, and Loss keeps its true value.
Changed from the plan: the trail marks every step (up to 200), not every 2nd, so the zigzag stays visible.
Dragging moves the start point side to side only, and only before the first step. The full-batch path uses the current learning rate from the same start.
